figurative

/FIG-yuh-ruh-tiv/ — stress on FIG · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Language that is figurative uses words imaginatively, such as through comparison or symbolism, rather than stating something in its exact, literal sense.

When Dad calls the garage 'a black hole,' he is being figurative — mostly.

Example

When the coach said the team was 'on fire,' she was being figurative—the players weren't literally burning; they were playing brilliantly.

Figure + -ative (the silent e drops): inclined to use figures of speech. Figurative language uses words imaginatively—through metaphor, simile, symbolism, or personification—rather than literally. The sentence shows the coach's words as symbolic (fire = excellent performance) rather than literal.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

metaphorical: Metaphorical language describes one thing as if it were another — calling homework a mountain, or grief a storm. Figurative is the umbrella term: it covers metaphor along with simile, personification, symbolism, and every other non-literal device. All metaphorical language is figurative, but not the reverse.

poetic: Poetic describes language with the music and craft of poetry — rhythm, vivid images, careful sound. Poetic lines can still be literally true. Figurative is about meaning rather than beauty: the words say one thing to mean another, whether or not they sound lovely doing it.

idiomatic: Idiomatic expressions are fixed phrases whose meaning cannot be worked out word by word — 'raining cats and dogs' is idiomatic. Figurative covers fresh, invented departures from literal meaning too, not just inherited set phrases. An idiom is figurative language a whole community has already agreed on.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

literal: meaning exactly what the words say

plain: direct, without imaginative decoration

Where it sits · how far words leave literal meaning — expressive → imaginative → symbolic → figurative

expressive vs. figurative: 'Expressive' language shows feeling, but figurative language goes further, saying one thing to mean another.

imaginative vs. figurative: An imaginative phrase is creative; a figurative one fully leaves literal meaning behind.

symbolic vs. figurative: 'Symbolic' lets one image stand for an idea; figurative is the broadest, bending words away from their plain sense through metaphor and exaggeration.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — figur-

Root — figur-: figure, shape — from Latin figura; the silent e drops before the suffix (Latin)

Suffix — -ative

Suffix — -ative: having the quality or tendency of (variant of -ive) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Figure drops its silent e and takes the -ative form of the suffix: having the quality of a figure of speech — using words imaginatively, through metaphor or exaggeration, rather than literally.

Use the root in a new word: figurine

Use the root in a new word: figurine: A tiny glass figurine of a dolphin sat on her windowsill.

Word Choice

neutral

Use figurative when describing language, writing, or speech that uses metaphor, simile, personification, symbolism, or other non-literal devices to create imagery or express ideas creatively. It's a staple of poetry, storytelling, and rhetorical language.
